events.text: The barrier of the Valley of a Hundred Beasts parts like warm breath. Inside, the air smells of musk and wet fern, and the grass is flattened in paths too wide for any deer. Somewhere ahead, a hundred throats go quiet at once, the way a forest does when it is listening to you.

effects.log: You keep the breeze in your face. The watchers lose your scent for a while, and you learn to move the way they do.
You stride in openly. Nothing attacks a creature that walks like it belongs. Something large follows you at a polite distance for an hour.

choices.text: Mark the trees as you go

effects.log: You notch the bark every hundred paces. Later you find the notches licked smooth, as if something wanted to know what you were.

events.text: Bones lie along the first stream, old and clean and sorted by size, as if someone had tidied them. A cracked wooden sign hangs on a post above them, its paint long gone. Only the carved outline survives: an open hand, palm up, the old sign for coming in peace.

choices.text: Lay your palm on the sign

effects.log: The wood is warm. When you take your hand away, a pair of yellow eyes in the ferns blinks once and withdraws.
Wolf, boar, deer, a bear's jaw. No human bones at all. Whatever keeps this valley buries its own kind and leaves the rest.
You pocket a wolf's fang. The valley goes quiet behind you, and stays quiet, and you feel watched all morning.

events.text: The smell reaches you first: musk, fern, the cold mineral breath of the stream. You have never stood here in this life, and your feet already know where the ground is soft. A past life walked this valley with care. Something in you is bracing for the white ape's call long before it comes.

effects.log: They take you around a sinkhole you could not have seen. Your soul, it seems, remembers falling in.

choices.text: Whisper a greeting to the ferns

effects.log: Nothing answers. But nothing hunts you either, all that first day, and the birds do not flee.

events.text: At the mouth of the valley you stop, and for a long moment you cannot make yourself go on. Your hands are cold. You know, without knowing how, that you died somewhere past the second ridge, and that the last thing you saw was white fur against a red sky.

effects.log: You walk to the place where the fear is strongest. It is only a clearing with a split boulder. You touch the stone, and the old death lets go of you a little.
You take the long way round the second ridge. It costs you half a day, and you do not mind.

events.text: The crack you slip through is a beast's own door: a gap in the barrier worn smooth at shoulder height by animals going in and out for centuries. Coarse grey hairs cling to its edges. Whatever made it is larger than you, and it uses this door every night.

choices.text: Rub the hairs on your sleeves

effects.log: You smell of the valley now. A lynx on a branch above looks at you and decides you are family.
You are a hundred paces in when something squeezes through the gap behind you. You do not look back. It does not follow.

events.text: The safe road and the beast road both pass the same hot spring, and every creature in the valley seems to know it. Deer stand shoulder to shoulder with a tiger at the water's edge, drinking. Nobody hunts at the spring. It is the one law of the valley, and it is older than any sect.

effects.log: You kneel between a doe and a badger. The water tastes of iron and something sweet. The tiger watches you drink and does not stop drinking.
You sit on a rock until the last fawn has wandered off. When you finally drink, the spring is yours alone, and very quiet.

choices.text: Fill your flask and move on

effects.log: You do not linger. The tiger lifts its head as you go, water dripping from its chin, and watches you all the way to the trees.

events.text: Halfway through the valley you find a camp left in a hurry: a cold fire, a torn tent, iron nets tangled on the ground and a dozen empty cages with their doors bent outward. Something let the beasts out. Something with hands, judging by the neatly lifted latches.

effects.log: Under the tent lies a purse of silver and a poacher's tally of creatures caught. Every line has been struck through in a different ink.
The iron does not burn, but the ropes do. A raven watches the smoke from a branch and seems satisfied.
You step around the cages. Whoever opened them may come back for whoever set them, and you would rather not be standing here.

events.text: The beast road is a tunnel of thorn and root, too low to stand in. You crawl. Twice something breathes on the back of your neck and moves on. Once a she-bear with two cubs blocks the way and stares at you until your knees ache, then grunts and shoulders past, close enough to brush.

effects.log: You do not breathe. The cubs sniff your boots. When they are gone you realise you learned more about stillness in one breath than in a year of sitting.
You give ground. The bear accepts the apology and the cubs tumble after her. Your sleeve is torn on the thorns, and nothing else.

events.text: The hidden road begins behind a waterfall your feet remember. Behind the falling water is a ledge, on the ledge a cairn, and in the cairn a bundle in oiled cloth that your own hands tied a lifetime ago. Wolves on the far bank watch you unwrap it. They have the look of animals whose grandmothers knew you.

effects.log: You tuck a coin and a strip of your sleeve into the cairn, for whoever you will be next time.
You empty the cairn to the last stone. The wolves turn and trot off, as if the visit is over.

events.text: The white ape's ledge is behind you now, and the valley seems to breathe out. On the way down you pass a ring of stones where a dozen monkeys sit grooming each other. They stop to look at you, all together, and you have the strange feeling that a verdict is being passed.

effects.log: The oldest one bares its teeth, which may be a smile. The rest go back to grooming.
You keep your eyes on the path. Behind you the chattering starts again, louder, and sounds a great deal like laughter.

events.text: When it is over you sit on a root and shake for a while. You have faced fighters with swords. You have never faced anything that looked at you the way the white ape did: without hatred, without hunger, only a vast tiredness, as if it has done this for three hundred years and expects to do it for three hundred more.

effects.log: Not treasure, you decide. Nobody guards treasure that long. It is guarding a promise.
Dried meat and cold rice. Your hands stop shaking by the third mouthful.

events.text: The white ape goes down onto one knee the way an old person does, slowly, a hand on the ground. It is breathing hard. It looks at the fist-sized core of amber light in the hollow behind it, then at you, and moves aside. You have the feeling it is relieved.

effects.log: Its hand is enormous and leathery and very gentle in yours. It lets you help, then walks off into the trees on two legs, like a tired grandparent going to bed.

choices.text: Take the core and go quickly

effects.log: You do not wait to see if it changes its mind. The core is warm in your hands, and pulses like a heart.

choices.text: Ask it what it was guarding

effects.log: It looks past you, at a slope of small grave mounds you had not noticed. Then it closes its eyes.

events.text: The ape does not finish you. It knocks you down, again and again, each blow measured, until you stop getting up. Then it sits beside you on the ledge and picks the leaves out of your hair while you lie there, the way it must once have done for children who climbed too high.

effects.log: When it is done it grunts, pats your head twice and climbs back to its watch. You have lost. You do not feel beaten.
You drag yourself off the ledge. It watches you go with sad brown eyes, and lets you.

events.text: You go past the white ape's ledge flat on your belly in the long grass, an hour for every hundred paces. Once it turns its great head your way and sniffs. Then it turns back to the valley it guards. You are almost certain it knew you were there, and decided you were not worth the trouble.

effects.log: Perhaps it is. Perhaps it is pity. Either way you are past.
Not worth the trouble. You carry the thought all the way to the gate and find it makes you walk taller.

events.text: You are halfway across the ledge when a hand the size of a shovel closes on your ankle and lifts you into the air. The white ape holds you upside down at eye level, studies you for a long swinging moment, and tosses you into the ferns, as one throws back a fish too small to keep.

choices.text: Try again from the other side

effects.log: You try. It is waiting there too, and this time it only shakes its head at you. You give up and go round.
Too small to keep. You laugh at yourself all the way down the valley, and it does you good.

events.text: You sit down in front of the white ape and do nothing at all for a very long time. When it finally comes close, you hold out your hand with the palm open, the old Hwang sign carved on every post in the valley. The ape stares at your hand. Then it takes it, sets it on its own head, and closes its eyes.

effects.log: The fur is coarse and white and warm. It leans into your hand like a dog. When you stand, it pushes the core toward you with one knuckle.

choices.text: Ask it to come with you

effects.log: It looks toward the grave mounds on the slope, then back at you, and gently shakes its head. Some guardians cannot leave.

events.text: You hold out your open palm, the way the signs in the valley show. The ape looks at it, then at you, and something old and grieving comes into its face. It turns its back and will not look at you again. Whoever last held out a hand to it like that, you are not them.

effects.log: You hold it out until your arm shakes. The ape does not turn. At last you lower it.
You leave it to its grief. Halfway down the slope you hear it call once, long and low, toward the graves.

events.text: The closing gate of the valley is a wall of mist, and the beasts gather to watch the outsiders leave: deer on the ridge, wolves in the ferns, a line of crows on a dead pine. As the last of you steps through, a hundred animal voices rise together, and for a long time you cannot tell whether it was a farewell or a warning.

effects.log: You shout back into the mist. The valley falls silent at once. Then a single wolf answers you.
The voices follow you to the barrier and stop there, cut off as if by a closing door.

events.text: Outside the gate, merchants have set up stalls in the mud: bandages, hot buns, and cages, rows of empty cages with prices chalked on them. A man in a fur hat calls out that he pays well for live cubs, better for cores, and asks no questions. The beasts' smell is still on your clothes. A few of the cages already rattle.

effects.log: A marten shoots out of it and into the woods. The man in the fur hat swears, and decides you are not worth a fight.
He names them. You remember them, the way one remembers the price of a life. You buy nothing and sell nothing.
You walk past the cages and do not look at what is in them. It is harder than it should be.

events.text: Your sect's elders take the beast core from you in a lacquered box, already arguing over which disciple's pill it will go into. Nobody asks about the ape. Nobody asks how it looked at you, or what it was guarding. You find you mind that more than giving up the core.

effects.log: The eldest elder listens, to your surprise, to the end. Incense will be sent to the valley, it is decided, and written down.
Some things do not belong in a record book. You keep the ape for yourself.

events.text: The fighters waiting outside the gate wear iron rings sewn into their coats and carry weighted nets instead of swords: poachers, not bandits, used to catching things that bite. Whatever happened in the fight, you saw their leader clearly. A broad, patient face. The face of a man who waits outside every opening.

effects.log: You will know it again. Next time, he will not see you first.

choices.text: Ask the gate guards about him

effects.log: "Iron-Net Gwak," says a guard, and spits. "Buys from everyone, robs the rest. Nobody has ever caught him."

events.text: A snare snaps shut on the path ahead, and a young woman drops out of the oak above it, swearing. She is perhaps nineteen, with a knife in her teeth and a fox kit squirming in her jacket. 'Cha Bom,' she says around the knife. 'I come in every opening to undo what the poachers do. Help me, or step aside.'

effects.log: You spend the morning on your knees cutting wire. Bom works faster than you and talks the whole time, mostly about foxes.
Bom looks at you as if you were a snare yourself. "Enough," she says, and is gone into the oaks before you can say it was a joke.
She is gone into the ferns before you finish nodding. The fox kit looks back at you over her shoulder.

events.text: Cha Bom finds you after the ape's ledge, picking burrs out of your hair before you can object. 'You met Grandfather, then,' she says. 'That is what my village called it. The Hwang beast-keepers raised it from a baby, three hundred years back, and the governor burned them for refusing to train war-beasts. It still guards their graves.'

effects.log: She leads you to a hillside of small mounds, each with a carved animal on it instead of a name. You leave a handful of grain at the biggest, and a sparrow takes it.
"My grandmother was the last Hwang child," she says, "smuggled out in a grain sack." She says it lightly. Her hands stop moving while she does.

events.text: At the closing gate Cha Bom catches your sleeve. Her jacket is empty; the fox kit has gone home. 'Gwak waits outside every opening to buy what people carry out,' she says. 'Cores, cubs, anything. He will offer you a fortune one day. I am asking you never to sell him anything from this valley.'

effects.log: Bom grins, the first time you have seen it. She presses a carved wooden fox into your palm and vanishes into the crowd at the gate.
"Fair," she says, and lets go of your sleeve. "At least you do not lie." She is gone before the gate finishes closing.

events.text: A broad man in an iron-ringed coat steps out of the crowd at the gate and falls in beside you as if you were old partners. 'Iron-Net Gwak,' he says. 'A little fox told me you asked about my prices. I do not buy only cubs. I buy knowledge. Where does the she-bear den? Where do the wolves raise their young?'

effects.log: He counts silver into your hand without haggling. That night you dream of empty cages with their doors shut.
You describe a den on the far side of the valley in loving detail. It is a wasps' nest. He thanks you warmly.
He shrugs, unoffended. "Everyone sells, in the end," he says, and is gone into the crowd.

events.text: The Ruins of the Nameless Sect sit on a mountain shoulder above the clouds: roofless halls, a cracked bell, a training yard where grass grows between flagstones worn hollow by ten thousand feet. Every plaque over every door has been chiselled blank. Somebody went to great trouble to make sure you would never know where you are.

effects.log: Under your fingers the stone is rough with the scars of a chisel, struck by a hand that did not shake.
It is cracked from lip to crown. You tap it with a knuckle and it gives back a dull, broken note that carries a surprisingly long way.
You stand in one of the worn hollows. It fits your feet. You take the stance it was made for without meaning to.

events.text: Snow lies in the corners of the halls, though it is summer outside. In the main hall a long row of meditation cushions has rotted to grey threads, and on each one lies a small pile of ash, neatly swept. The ash of letters, by the curl of it. Each disciple burned a name, sitting in their own place.

choices.text: Bow to the row of cushions

effects.log: You bow once to the whole row. It feels like the right number.
Most of it is dust. One flake holds half a brushstroke. You cannot read it, and you put it back.
The last one in the row has no ash. You sit. The cold comes up through you, and with it a great patience.

events.text: You know this hall. Not the ruin of it: the hall as it was, warm, lamps lit, a voice reading aloud. The memory is gone as soon as you reach for it, and the roofless walls are only walls again. But your feet have turned you, without asking, toward the third door on the left.

effects.log: A small room, a broken desk, a window onto the clouds. You stand where someone once stood every morning, and do not know why your eyes sting.
Some doors are better left. You walk the other way, and the feeling follows you like a dog that knows you.

events.text: On the steps of the guardian's hall there is a place where the moss will not grow, a patch the shape of a person lying down. You know whose it is. A past life of yours fell there, asking the wrong question of the last disciple. Your knees go weak at the sight of it, and then, slowly, steady again.

choices.text: Lay a stone on the patch

effects.log: A small grave for a self you do not remember. It is enough.

choices.text: Wonder what the wrong question was

effects.log: You do not know. But you know now that there is a wrong one, and that is more than you knew in the other life.

events.text: The stairs up to the ruins are steep and very long, and your knees tell you about every one. Younger fighters pass you two steps at a time. On the last step you find a scrap of paper held down by a pebble. In a shaky old hand someone has written: 'Rest here. The disciple does not mind waiting.'

effects.log: You sit on the step and breathe. A cloud drifts past at the level of your feet. Nobody hurries you.

choices.text: Add a line of your own

effects.log: Under the old line you write: "Neither does the ruin." You leave the pebble where you found it.

events.text: The safe road runs through the old library. The shelves are empty, every one, and swept clean; not a scrap of bamboo slip is left. But on the walls, faded almost to nothing, someone painted the sect's arts as pictures: a figure stepping, turning, striking. No names, no words. The sect kept the art and burned the name.

effects.log: You trace the figures with your eyes until they move behind your eyelids. There is a footstep in them you have never seen anywhere else.
You practise the first figure on the dusty floor. It is harder than it looks, and better.

events.text: Rival parties pass you in the ruined corridors, quiet and careful. Nobody fights in these halls. A disciple of some far sect tells you why in a whisper: at the first opening, two parties fought in the library, and the last disciple came out of its hall for the first and only time. Neither party left. Now everyone walks softly.

effects.log: You keep your blade sheathed and your voice low, and the ruin lets you pass.
"Better not," the stranger says. "Not here." But at the next corner a ration cake is waiting on a ledge for you.

events.text: The beast road is the mountain's outer wall, a ledge above nothing, where the ruins' wild goats live. They have lived without people so long they have forgotten fear. One butts you in the back on the narrowest stretch, hard, to see what you will do.

effects.log: You wrestle it to a standstill on the edge of the cloud. It looks at you with new respect and lets you go first.
You flatten yourself to the wall. It trots by, satisfied, and you follow its hoofprints, which know the ledge better than you do.

events.text: The hidden road goes under the ruins, through the old storerooms, which your feet find in the dark. In a niche behind the third grain jar is a lacquer box you hid there a lifetime ago. Inside, wrapped in silk, is a stack of practice notes in a hand that is not your hand now, but was.

effects.log: A disciple's notes, full of crossings-out. Someone struggled with the same footwork painted on the library wall. You recognise the mistakes as your own.
You will read it later, somewhere warm. For now it is enough to know you once left yourself a gift.

events.text: Afterwards you sit in the doorway of the guardian's hall and look out over the clouds. Three hundred years ago an army came up this mountain. You try to picture being the one who stayed at this door, ordered to keep it, while everyone else burned their names and walked out to meet the army.

choices.text: Sit the watch for an hour

effects.log: You keep the door for one hour, for no reason but that someone kept it for three hundred years.
The ruins are no place to be when the light goes. You go down quickly, and the clouds close behind you.

events.text: The guardian's hall has one window, and through it the whole range is white with snow, though you came in under a summer sky. Beside the window hangs the only writing left in the ruins: 'Keep the door until someone asks the right question.' The door is kept. The question, it seems, is still unasked.

effects.log: You turn questions over all the way down the mountain. None of them feels right. All of them make you think.
Some riddles belong to the dead. You bow to the scroll and go.

events.text: The last disciple drops its sword of grey light, and the sword is gone before it touches the floor. It kneels, slowly, and sets a half-burned book on the boards between you, pushing it forward with two fingers like a student handing in work. Then it stands and goes back to its door. It is not defeated. It has only finished one more duty.

choices.text: Bow to it before you take the book

effects.log: It returns the bow exactly. For a moment, in the grey light, you see a young face, no older than a junior disciple.

choices.text: Take the book and ask its name

effects.log: It shakes its head. It has no name; none of them do. That was the price they paid.

events.text: The last disciple beats you with a style you have never seen, simple and terribly patient, and when you are down it stops at once. It does not strike again. It points at the door. Then it says, in a voice like wind through a crack, the only word you will hear from it: 'Again.' Not a threat. A teacher's word.

effects.log: You lie on the boards and go over the fight. There was a footstep you have never seen. You will see it in your sleep for years.
It nods once. It has heard that before, you think, from many people. It waits anyway.

events.text: You slip through the guardian's hall in a pillar's shadow while the last disciple stands at its door with its back to you, watching the clouds. Once it turns its head and you freeze. It looks straight at your pillar, then turns back. Three hundred years watching the door, and nobody ever asked it to watch the room.

effects.log: A guard so faithful it never learned to look behind itself. You leave a stick of incense burning by the pillar.
Every art has a back it does not watch. You will remember that.

events.text: Your foot finds the one loose board in the hall. The last disciple turns, crosses the floor without seeming to move, and taps you once on the forehead with the flat of its grey sword, gently, like a master correcting a child. The tap hurts more than any blow you have taken. Then it points at the door.

effects.log: Walk where the floor has been walked. You go out the way you came in, and you will not forget which board.
It does not bow back. But it waits until you are out of sight before it turns to its door.

events.text: As the ruins close, the snow in the halls melts all at once, and the water runs down the stairs ahead of you as if the mountain were weeping. At the bottom the gate is a sheet of mist. Behind you the cracked bell rings once, though no one is near it.

effects.log: The ruin is already fading. The last thing you see is the guardian's door, still shut, still kept.
Nine echoes off nine peaks. You do not know what it means, and you keep the number anyway.

events.text: At the gate a dozen parties wait to leave, and nobody speaks of what they found. One young swordsman sits apart, staring at his feet. He saw the library paintings, he tells you, and now his feet keep moving in that pattern on their own. 'Is that normal?' he asks. It is not. It is what the ruin does.

effects.log: You take the pattern one step further. He follows, and his face clears, as if he has been holding his breath for a day.

choices.text: Tell him to write it down

effects.log: "Before it goes," you say. He scrabbles in his pack for a brush. By the time the gate opens he has filled four pages.

events.text: Your sect's elders read the half-burned manual in a locked room for three days and come out arguing. Half of it is a body art, they say, and the other half is ash. One elder wants to burn the rest, since half an art is a dangerous thing. Another wants to rebuild the missing half from guesses. They ask what you think.

effects.log: The guessing begins. It will take the sect ten years, and every disciple will curse your name in the practice yard.
"Half of a true thing," you say, "is better than a whole false one." The eldest nods, and the book goes into the vault untouched.

events.text: The ambush at the gate is quick and quiet. Afterward, among the dropped weapons, you find a tablet of plain wood with a real sect's name burned into it, nothing to do with the ruins. Whoever sent them wanted you to know exactly who they were. Or wanted you to think so.

effects.log: You remember the name. Some day it will be settled.
Nobody brings a calling card to an ambush. Somebody wants two sects at each other's throats. You keep the tablet and your silence.

events.text: In the gatehouse an old man stands on a ladder, a lamp in one hand, taking a rubbing of a chiselled plaque with the other. 'Yeo Seon-u,' he says without turning. 'Historian. No sect. Seventy-three years old. This is my fifth opening and I still do not know what this place was called. Hold the lamp, would you?'

effects.log: You hold it for an hour while he works. The chisel marks come up grey on the paper, and under them, almost, the ghost of a character. He gives you a copy for your trouble.
"Because someone tried so hard to make it not matter," he says. "Nobody burns a name that meant nothing." He gives you a rubbing anyway, in case.
He does not seem to notice you go. His lamp is still burning in the gatehouse when you look back.

events.arc: The Historian of the Nameless Sect

events.text: When it is over, the last disciple of the Nameless Sect stands in the dim hall, flickering. It sees the corner of Yeo's rubbing in your sleeve and goes still. Then it reaches out one finger of grey light and, beside the half-character on the paper, writes a second. The sect's name. It looks at you as if it has set down something heavy.

effects.log: It inclines its head, an old disciple's bow, and goes back to its watch. The two characters on the paper are still faintly warm.

choices.text: Ask why it never told anyone

effects.log: It points at the rubbing, then at you. Nobody ever asked, you understand; they came for the manual. You are the first to bring it the name half-written.

events.arc: The Historian of the Nameless Sect

events.text: Yeo Seon-u is sitting on the gatehouse steps when you come out, wrapped in two coats, looking older than he did this morning. He reads your face before the rubbing. 'You have it,' he says. 'Fifty years. Show me.' Then he stops, and puts his hands in his sleeves. 'Or do not. They burned it themselves. Perhaps they meant it.'

effects.log: He reads the two characters three times, moving his lips. Then he folds the paper into his robe and weeps, quite openly. He will put it in a book, you know. The world will learn the name.

choices.text: Burn the rubbing in front of him

effects.log: He watches the paper curl. "Yes," he says at last, quietly. "That was what they wanted." He shakes your hand and walks down the mountain alone.

choices.text: Show him, and ask him to keep it secret

effects.log: He reads it, and nods slowly. "One old man knowing is not a world knowing," he says. "I can keep that."

events.arc: The Historian of the Nameless Sect

events.text: The Spirit Spring opens at dusk, always at dusk, and you step through the barrier into a mountain hollow full of mist and stone lanterns. Nobody has lit them in a century. They glow anyway, faintly, a soft blue light that seems to come from the water running beneath them.

effects.log: They lead you uphill, one after another, like someone walking ahead of you with a lamp.
It is cold and sweet and full of qi. Your meridians tingle down to your fingertips.

events.text: A stone path climbs past a little hermitage with a moss roof. Inside, on a shelf, sits a row of tiny clay cups, one for each of the nuns who lived here, their names scratched into the bases. All but one are turned upside down. The last cup stands upright, waiting, as if its owner only stepped out.

effects.log: You turn it gently. Something in the hermitage seems to settle, like a held breath let go.
Some waiting is not yours to end. You close the door softly behind you.
Twenty-two names. The last is the abbess's, scratched deeper than the rest. Someone pressed hard.

events.text: You know the taste of the water before it touches your lips. A past life knelt at this spring, and drank, and saw something in the moon's reflection that made it weep. You do not remember what. But the moment you kneel, your hands cup themselves the old way, fingers tight, and not a drop is lost.

effects.log: In the water's surface, for a breath, there is a face that is not quite yours, smiling at you as at an old friend.
Whatever that life saw, it can keep. The water is cold and very good.

events.text: The deep pool at the heart of the spring is clear to the bottom, and on the bottom, among white pebbles, lies a rusted sword hilt. You know it. Your hand knows the wrap of it. A past life went into that water after the jade carp and did not come up, and the carp, it seems, kept the hilt.

effects.log: The water is so cold it burns. You come up with the hilt and nothing else, gasping, and somehow lighter.
It is a grave now. You drop a white pebble of your own beside it.

events.text: The crack in the spring's barrier is underwater: a pale gap in a rock pool, and you have to swim through it. You surface inside, gasping, among lily pads as broad as tables. A frog the size of a dog watches you climb out, unimpressed.

effects.log: You are cold to the bone, and the mist is colder. You keep moving, which helps.
It hops off toward the north. You follow it, because why not, and it is the right way.

events.text: The road to the spring's heart follows a stream so clear you can count the pebbles. Silver fish hang in the current, all facing upstream, perfectly still, as if listening to something you cannot hear. When you stop walking, they turn all at once to look at you.

effects.log: You stand until your breathing matches the current. Then you hear it too: very far away, a bell.
The fish turn back upstream. You never hear the bell, but you walk a little lighter.

events.text: A lantern has fallen across the path and cracked open. Inside it is not oil but a little pool of glowing water, and in the water the reflection of a full moon, though the sky above is black. Someone has dropped a stone into it to see what happens. The moon's reflection simply moved over.

effects.log: You lift it carefully. The moon swirls and settles, and the lantern's glow brightens a little.
It tastes of cold nights and silver. For a moment the whole sky above you is full of moons.

events.text: The beast road goes through the reed beds where the spring's water snakes live: thick as your arm, green as jade, and quite unafraid. They do not bite. They only coil around your legs as you wade, one after another, and squeeze, very gently, as if measuring you.

effects.log: The last one lets go with what you would swear is a nod. You have passed a test you did not know you were taking.
You splash through in a hurry. One snake, offended, nips your ankle, and the cold of it runs up your leg for an hour.

events.text: Your feet take you off the path and up a goat track to a ledge behind the hermitage, where a flat stone covers a hollow. Inside, wrapped in a nun's grey scarf, is a little gourd you filled at the spring a lifetime ago and never came back for. It is still full. The water inside still glows faintly.

effects.log: It tastes of an old life's patience. You drink it all.
You tie the gourd to your belt. Some gifts should not be finished in a hurry.

events.text: Afterwards the deep pool is still again, and in its surface the moon hangs perfectly, though there is no moon in the sky. You stand at the edge until your feet are numb. A carp that size must have eaten a great deal of moonlight. Someone must have fed it, every night, for a very long time.

choices.text: Feed the pool a rice cake

effects.log: It sinks slowly, glowing. Far down, a pale shape rises to meet it, takes it, and is gone.
You walk away backwards, as one leaves a temple. The moon in the water watches you go.

events.text: On the stones at the pool's edge someone carved a little poem long ago, nearly hidden under moss. You scrape it clean with your thumbnail: 'Every night I gave you the moon. Every night you gave it back.' Beneath it are the abbess's seal and a small carved fish.

effects.log: You say it under your breath down the length of the stream. By the bottom, you understand it.

choices.text: Carve your own mark beside it

effects.log: A small mark beside the fish. It will be moss by the next opening.

events.text: The jade carp turns on its side at last and lies on the surface like a fallen boat, gills working. It is not dead. It is very old and very tired, and it has lost. Its huge golden eye rolls to look at you, and then at a gourd wedged between the stones at the water's edge, half hidden in the reeds.

choices.text: Push it back into the deep

effects.log: It takes all your strength. When it slips under, it leaves a long curl of moonlight on the water behind it, like thanks.
The gourd is cold and heavy. Behind you the carp sinks by itself, slowly, out of sight.

events.text: The carp's tail hits you like a falling door, and you go into the water, and down. Beneath the surface it is quiet and full of blue light. A golden eye regards you. Then something nudges you upward, gently, until you break the surface coughing and crawl out onto the stones. It let you go. It always lets them go.

choices.text: Lie on the stones and breathe

effects.log: You lie there until the shaking stops. The pool is smooth again, as if nothing happened.
Someone fed this fish every night for a hundred years. Some of their kindness stayed in the water.

events.text: You wait until the moon's reflection drifts to the far side of the pool and the great pale shape follows it, as it does every hour, like a dog after a ball. Then you cross the stepping stones in seven long strides. The carp never turns. It has chased that moon for a hundred years and never once caught it.

effects.log: To chase the same moon every night. You think of a few people you know who do the same.
Every guardian has a habit. This one kept you dry.

events.text: The fourth stepping stone is not a stone. It is a fin. The carp rises under you and you are thrown, quite gently, back onto the bank you started from, wet to the skin. The great fish settles into the deep. You could swear it is laughing.

effects.log: You sit on the bank dripping and laughing, and some of the fear goes out of you with it.
You go through the reeds instead. It costs you an hour and both sandals.

events.text: You kneel at the pool's edge and, without knowing why, hum the old moon-watching song every village knows. The great carp rises slowly and lays its head on the stones in front of you, and lets you touch it. Its scales are cold and smooth as jade. Something in its eye is very like a smile.

effects.log: You sing all of it. The carp listens to the last note, then noses the gourd out of the reeds toward your hand.
It cannot understand you. It seems to anyway. When you leave, it follows you along the bank as far as the water goes.

events.text: You hum the old moon song and hold out a rice cake. The carp rises, looks at the cake, looks at you, and sinks without taking it. It was fed by one hand for a hundred years. It does not want another.

choices.text: Leave the cake on the stones

effects.log: Perhaps it will take it later, when you are gone. Perhaps the moon will.
Some loyalties are not for sale, not even for a rice cake and a song. You respect it for that.

events.text: When the Spirit Spring closes, the stone lanterns go out one by one from the top of the hollow down, as if someone were walking ahead of you blowing them out. By the gate only the last one still burns. It stays lit until you have stepped through, and then it goes out too.

effects.log: Nobody answers. But the mist outside the gate smells faintly of incense.
The hollow is black and silent. For a moment twenty-two small lights move up the hill, and then nothing.

events.text: Outside the gate, villagers wait with buckets and jars, hoping to buy a cup of spring water from anyone coming out. An old farmer offers you a whole string of coins for a mouthful. A girl offers you a hen. Behind them, at a respectful distance, a monk waits with an empty bowl and offers nothing at all.

effects.log: He drinks, closes his eyes, and says, "The moon," as if greeting an old friend. Then he walks off without another word.
He pays without haggling and drinks it on the spot. Whatever he hoped for, you hope he finds.
You shoulder through the buckets. The girl with the hen calls you something rude, and she has a point.

events.text: Your sect's alchemists take the gourd of moon-remembering water with shaking hands and pour it into crystal flasks the size of a thumb. It makes forty. They give one back to you, because you carried it, and say the rest will go to forty breakthroughs. You think of the carp, chasing its moon.

effects.log: You drink it on the sect's rooftop that night, under the real moon. The two moons, one inside you and one above, feel like the same thing.

choices.text: Give it to a struggling junior

effects.log: The junior breaks through a month later and tells everyone who will listen why.

events.text: The robbers at the spring's gate are ragged and thin and their blades are rusty, and when it is over one of them, a boy of perhaps fifteen, sits in the mud and sobs that he only wanted water for his village. He does not seem to be lying. The others have already fled.

effects.log: You pour a little into his cupped hands. He drinks, stops crying, and runs off toward the villages.
The guards take him away. He looks back at you once, and you remember it.
You jerk your chin at the woods. He goes, fast.

events.text: At a bend in the stream a woman in a village headscarf is scooping spring water into clay jars, very fast, glancing over her shoulder. She has no weapon and no sect badge, and her sandals are soaked. 'Please,' she says. 'Pyo Ok-rye, from the valley farms. Do not tell the guards. My boy has a cough that will not stop.'

effects.log: You fill four jars together. Her hands shake. Her son is called Dal-i, she tells you, and is nine, and likes frogs.
"Stay away from the deep pool," you tell her. She nods, and you can see she will go anyway, if the jars are not enough.
You walk on. Behind you the sound of scooping water does not stop.

events.text: When the guardian is behind you, a cry comes from the deep pool. Pyo Ok-rye is up to her waist in the water, a jar in each hand, and something enormous and pale is turning beneath her, slowly, like a cloud. The carp. It has not struck. It is looking at her.

effects.log: You wade in and haul her back by the collar. The carp rises behind you, close enough that you feel its cold, then sinks away. Ok-rye clutches the jars and will not stop thanking you.
She freezes. The carp circles her once, twice, then gently noses one of her jars, as if to say: that one. Then it is gone.

events.text: At the closing gate, Ok-rye is turned back by the sect guards: no badge, no water leaving the realm without their tithe. Her jars are taken. She stands in the mist with empty hands. You have water too, in your own flask, and the guards are not checking you.

effects.log: She takes it in both hands and bows so low her scarf touches the mud. You think about Dal-i and his frogs for a long time.

ok.log: "One jar," the guard says at last, sick of you. "One." Ok-rye runs.

fail.log: They will not hear it. Ok-rye goes home with nothing, and you carry her thanks home anyway, which is worse.

effects.log: You drink it yourself on the road down. It is very good water.

events.text: The Bandit King's Vault is a mountain hollowed out like a melon. Torches flare to life by themselves as you pass, set in brackets shaped like grinning tigers. The air smells of old iron and older smoke. Somewhere far inside, slow and heavy and regular, something made of metal is walking.

effects.log: Forty paces, a turn, forty paces back. It has walked the same round so long the floor must be worn into a groove.
The tiger bracket lets go of it with a click. The flame does not flicker, even when you run.

events.text: Carved into the wall at the entrance, in letters as tall as a person, are the Bandit King's three laws: Never rob the poor. Never rob the same barge twice. Never leave a debt unpaid. Under the third, someone has scratched, much later, in a small mean hand: 'He owes me fifty taels.'

effects.log: Three hundred years on, the debts of the dead are still being argued over.
For a bandit, they are better laws than some governors keep. You find you mean it.

events.text: You know where the trap is before you see it: the third flagstone past the tiger torches, which sinks a finger's width and drops a grille behind it. A past life of yours stepped on it, you are sure, and spent a whole night behind that grille. Your feet still remember the cold.

effects.log: You step over it neatly. A rival party behind you does not, and you hear the grille come down, and some very bad language.
You wedge a stone under it so it cannot sink. Somebody behind you will never know you saved them a cold night.

events.text: Deep in the vault a side tunnel ends where the floor drops into darkness. You stop at the edge and cannot go closer. You fell here. You do not know how you know it, only that it was this exact edge, and that someone's hand was on your back as you went over. Not the puppet's. A hand.

effects.log: You do not remember the face. But a soul does not forget a push. You go on more carefully, and you watch the people behind you.

choices.text: Throw a coin into the dark

effects.log: It falls for a long time. Far down it rings on stone, and the old fear goes with it.

events.text: The crack you sneak through is an old smugglers' chute, greased with three hundred years of grime, and you come down it far faster than you meant to and land in a heap of rotten sacks. Bandit King or no, somebody used this vault as a warehouse long after he died.

effects.log: Mostly rot. One sack holds a string of old copper coins, forgotten.
Chalk arrows, still faint on the walls. They lead the long way round the guard posts, and you follow them gratefully.

events.text: The safe road runs through the Bandit King's feasting hall, where once a year he fed every village headman in the province. The long tables are still set: bronze cups, bowls, chopsticks laid side by side. Dust lies on everything like grey snow. At the head of the table, the king's own chair faces the door.

effects.log: From here you can see every door. A good chair for a man who trusted nobody, and fed everyone anyway.
It is heavy and well made. It will sell. You feel the empty place it leaves at the table.

events.text: Rival parties are prising open chests along the safe road with crowbars, and finding them full of rocks. Every one. The Bandit King filled a hundred chests with rocks and painted one word inside each lid: 'Patience.' A disciple of some far sect is kicking a chest and weeping with rage.

choices.text: Help him open the next chest

effects.log: Rocks, and the same word. He sits down on the chest, and after a while you both start to laugh.
A hundred chests of rocks, and one true vault behind them. The king was teaching something. Whether anyone ever learned it is another question.

events.text: The beast road is the vault's flooded lower tunnels, where blind white eels the length of a spear hunt in black water. You wade with your blade drawn. You never see them. You feel them brush your legs, and once something wraps your ankle and tugs, hard, before letting go.

effects.log: You do not stop. By the far end your legs are numb and you have a story nobody will believe.
You go along the rough wall on fingers and toes, out of the water. It is slow and it skins your knuckles, and nothing touches you.

events.text: The hidden road begins behind a statue of a laughing tiger. You know which tooth to press. The statue swings aside, and in the hollow behind it is a pouch tied with a knot your hands made a lifetime ago. In it, with the silver, is a scrap of paper in your old hand: 'For next time. Do not trust the merchant.'

effects.log: Your past self does not say. Your present self resolves to trust no merchants at all, which is probably wise anyway.
You fold the scrap into your sleeve. A soul that leaves itself a warning learned the hard way.

events.text: The vault's inner door hangs open behind you now, and the iron puppet's footsteps have stopped. In the silence you notice a smith's handprint pressed into the iron of the wall while it was still soft. Under it, scratched small: 'Seok. Stayed by choice.' The Bandit King's captive smith, it seems, did not want to leave.

choices.text: Lay your hand on the print

effects.log: Your hand is smaller than the smith's. The iron is warm. Somebody loved this work.
Nobody stays in a bandit's mountain by choice, unless the bandit was better company than the world outside.

events.text: On the way back from the vault's heart you pass the iron puppet's workshop: a cold forge, hammers on hooks, and a dozen half-built iron hands on a bench, each a little better than the last. The last one is perfect. It is holding a small tin flower.

effects.log: It is light and cold and very carefully made. You do not know why it matters, only that it does.
Some things are made to be held, and not by you.
Each one moves a little better. The smith was learning how to make something that could hold a flower without crushing it.

events.text: The iron puppet goes down in sections: an arm, a knee, and at last the great square head, which rolls across the floor and comes to rest facing the saber on its rack. Its jaw grinds once more. 'Nobody takes the saber,' it says in the Bandit King's own voice, 'who would not give it away.' Then the light in its eyes goes out.

choices.text: Promise you would give it away

effects.log: You say it aloud to the dead iron. The saber seems a little lighter when you lift it.

choices.text: Take the saber without a word

effects.log: It is the best blade you have ever held, and it knows it.

events.text: The iron puppet does not tire and does not feel pain and does not stop, and after a while you are on the floor with one heavy iron foot planted beside your head. It holds there. Then it turns and walks back to its round, forty paces and back, as if you had never been there. It was never ordered to kill. Only to guard.

effects.log: Forty paces. A turn on the left heel. Forty back. A machine is a pattern, and patterns can be learned.
You drag yourself out. Behind you the footsteps go on, forty paces and back, without end.

events.text: You count the puppet's footsteps from the shadows: forty paces, turn, forty back. On the thirty-eighth you move. You are past it and into the inner vault before its heel comes round. Behind you the footsteps go on without a pause. It never knew.

effects.log: Thirty-eight steps. You will remember the number for a long time.
Forty paces and back for three hundred years, for a king long dead. You know people like that.

events.text: You miscount. The iron hand closes on the back of your collar on the thirty-ninth step and lifts you off the floor, and the puppet carries you, kicking, all the way back to the entrance, and sets you down there, quite gently. Then it goes back to its round.

effects.log: Carried out like a cat by the scruff. You will not be telling anyone this.
Thirty-nine, not thirty-eight. Next time you will move one step sooner.

events.text: As the vault closes, the tiger torches go out one by one from the inside out, and through the tunnels behind you rolls something that might be laughter: a big, rough, happy laugh. At the gate, a hundred chests of rocks stand stacked in the light, as if someone dragged them there to see the visitors out.

effects.log: A plain grey rock from a bandit king's chest. Patience, the lid said. You keep it on your desk for years.
Thieves have their honour. You salute it.

events.text: At the gate a dozen parties wait to leave, all swapping stories of chests full of rocks, and nobody is quite sure whether they were robbed or taught a lesson. A grizzled fighter who has been in four openings says the king's laugh is a little quieter every time. 'He is getting tired,' he says. 'Like the rest of us.'

effects.log: He tells stories until the gate opens. Half of them are true. The other half are better.
His flask holds something terrible: barley tea, boiled for a week. You share it anyway, and at the gate you part like old comrades.

events.text: Your sect's treasury master weighs the Bandit King's saber, frowns, weighs it again, and pronounces it worth more than the main hall. Then it goes straight to the vault, to hang on a wall and never be drawn. Nobody takes the saber who would not give it away, the puppet said. You gave it away. It does not feel the way you thought.

effects.log: The treasury master frowns, then hands you a key on a cord. You are the only disciple who has one.
Perhaps that is what the king meant. You do not need to hold a thing to have earned it.

events.text: The ambushers at the vault's gate wear black kite feathers in their hats: the Black Kite band, who claim to be the Bandit King's heirs and say everything in the vault is theirs by right. Their leader, a woman with a voice like gravel, shouts over the fight that the king would have wanted it so. You doubt the king would have wanted them at all.

effects.log: "Never rob the poor!" you roar. Some of them hesitate. A dead bandit's law still weighs more than you would think.
You will know the Black Kites again. They will know you too.

events.text: In the vault's first cavern a woman in a merchant's travelling coat is reading a ledger by a candle stub, comparing it against the chests along the walls. 'Heo Ran, of the Heo trading house,' she says. 'Ma Cheon-pil robbed my great-great-grandfather's barges in this valley. Every coin here with our seal on it is ours. I want it back.'

choices.text: Offer to help her find them

effects.log: She looks at you as if you had spoken a foreign tongue, then laughs. "Help? In a bandit's vault? Fine. Hold the candle."

choices.text: Point out it was tax money

effects.log: "The Heo house carried the governor's taxes," you say, "and skimmed them, I would guess." She shuts the ledger with a snap. "Everyone skimmed. Come along, then, honest one."
She does not look up. The candle stub burns lower behind you.

events.arc: The Ledger of the Heo House

events.text: Heo Ran stops at a junction where the tunnel walls are cut with tally marks, thousands of them. 'The villages,' she says slowly, reading her ledger and then the wall. 'He wrote down every village he gave to.' She runs her finger along the marks. 'He gave away more than he kept. My family's books never said that.'

effects.log: She is quiet for a long time. "Books do," she says at last, and writes a note in the margin of her ledger in very small letters.
"No," she agrees, too quickly. "A thief is a thief." But she copies down the tally marks before she moves on.

events.arc: The Ledger of the Heo House

events.text: At the closing gate Heo Ran carries two heavy purses of sealed coin and a face that cannot decide what it feels. 'The Heo house would have me bring all of it home,' she says. 'The tally marks would have me take it to the river villages. You were there. You decide.'

choices.text: Take it home to the Heo house

effects.log: She nods, relieved and ashamed in equal measure, and presses a share into your hand. "For the candle," she says.
"My great-great-grandfather is turning in his tomb," she says, and smiles. "Good." She sets off for the river that same day.
Half to the house, half to the river. She laughs. "A merchant's answer," she says, "from someone who is not a merchant."

events.arc: The Ledger of the Heo House

events.text: The Bamboo Labyrinth is green on every side and above, the stalks so tall and close that the sky is a thin bright crack overhead. The wind never stops. It hisses through the leaves, rises and falls, and after a while you notice it has a rhythm. Like breathing. Like a sword swung slowly by someone very patient.

effects.log: In as the leaves rise, out as they fall. After a hundred breaths you could walk with your eyes shut.
You notch the stalks as you pass. Within an hour the notches have grown closed, as if the maze heals itself.

events.text: At the first junction there is a stone bench, and on it a pair of old straw sandals worn through at the toes, and a note under a pebble: 'I walked it a hundred times and never reached the middle. You go.' The note is old. The sandals are older.

effects.log: They fit, more or less, and are very comfortable. Somebody walked a long way in them, and somehow they still want to walk.

choices.text: Leave a note of your own

effects.log: Under the old line you write: "I will try." You leave the pebble on both.

events.text: The wind in the maze is playing a rhythm your body knows. Not your mind: your wrists, your knees, which start to move with it before you can stop them. A past life walked this labyrinth, you understand, and walked it so many times that the form it is made of got into the bones.

effects.log: You stop deciding where to turn. Your feet decide. They are right every time.
You walk on your own choices, slowly, badly. It is your life this time, and you will learn this maze yourself.

events.text: In a clearing of cut bamboo a rusted sword stands upright in the earth, a faded sash knotted to its hilt. You know the knot. You tied it, in another life, the morning you came in here and did not come out. The wind swordsman's leaves were faster than you then. A lifetime later, your hands are shaking.

effects.log: You loosen the old knot and tie it again, the way you tie things in this life. The shaking stops.

choices.text: Leave the grave as it is

effects.log: You bow to it. Whoever you were, you were brave enough to come here. So are you.

events.text: The maze is no place for old knees: the paths twist, the roots trip, and the wind pushes. But after the first hour you notice that the young ones around you are lost and arguing, and you are not. You have been lost in enough places to know that a maze is mostly patience.

effects.log: Slow and steady. You pass three young parties sitting in a dead end, red-faced, arguing about maps.
They follow you sheepishly. At the next fork you choose the right way, and they look at you as though you were a sage.

events.text: Deep in the maze the paths begin to repeat, and you find yourself at the same stone lantern for the third time. Its base is scratched with hundreds of little tally marks. Everyone who comes here passes this lantern three times. Some have scratched their names. One has scratched: 'Turn left when the wind turns.'

effects.log: You wait, and the wind changes, and you turn left. The lantern does not come round again.
A small mark among hundreds. It feels like signing a guest book.

events.text: The safe road is full of rival parties roped together so as not to get separated. They look ridiculous, and they do not get separated. One party offers to tie you on. The wind takes people who walk alone, sometimes, their leader says. You do not ask what she means.

effects.log: It is slow and undignified. Nobody on your rope is lost when the road splits.
The wind hisses louder when you leave them. You keep a hand on your hilt and nothing happens, which is somehow worse.

events.text: The beast road through the bamboo belongs to the bamboo rats, fat and bold and as big as dogs, who chew tunnels of their own through the stalks. One sits up in front of you and chatters furiously, its cheeks full. Behind it is the only way forward.

effects.log: You toss a rice cake. It stuffs that into its cheeks with the rest and waddles off, which leaves the tunnel open.
It bites your boot and holds on for twenty paces. You arrive at the far side dragging a furious rat.

events.text: Your feet find the hidden road where the wind is quietest, a gap between two stalks your eyes would never notice. At its end, in a hollow stump, is a bamboo tube sealed with wax you sealed yourself in another life. Inside is a strip of paper in your old hand: the maze's first nine turns, and a note. 'The leaves strike from the left. Always.'

effects.log: From the left. Always. You say it under your breath until you reach the clearing.

choices.text: Seal a new note for next time

effects.log: You add a line of your own, seal it and put it back. One day you will be glad of it.

events.text: After the leaves have settled, the clearing at the maze's heart is very quiet, and you notice what you were too busy to see before: the bamboo around it was planted in a pattern. From the middle the stalks spiral out like the path of a sword through the air. The whole maze is a sword form. Someone planted an art so it would outlive him.

effects.log: You walk it slowly, from the centre out. By the end your arm is moving with you, cutting air.
The wind dies as you sit. For a moment the whole maze holds its breath, waiting to see what you will do.

events.text: In the clearing stands a stone stele with one line on it, in a strong old hand: 'I had no disciple worthy of the form, so I gave it to the bamboo, and the bamboo will give it to whoever walks all the way in.' Underneath, smaller: 'Do not cut my bamboo.'

effects.log: You bow. The wind ruffles your hair, and stops.
Even a great master had his worries. You decide you like him.

events.text: The swordsman of wind and leaves comes apart under your last stroke and falls as a shower of green, which spins in the air and settles into the shape of a bamboo flute at your feet. The wind stops for the first time since you came in. In the silence, very faintly, someone sighs, the way a teacher sighs when the student finally gets it right.

effects.log: It is warm, and lighter than any blade. When you hold it, the leaves around the clearing turn toward you.
You bow to the place the sigh came from. When you straighten, the wind is blowing again, gently.

events.text: The swordsman of wind and leaves cuts you a dozen times, each cut a stinging line like a paper edge, none of them deep. It is not trying to kill you. It is correcting you. Every cut lands where your guard was open. When you finally go down, you know exactly where all your openings are, and you wish you did not.

effects.log: Twelve cuts, twelve openings. You will close every one of them, if it takes years.
They are cool and soft. You lie there until you can breathe without stinging.

events.text: You go through the clearing in the wind's own rhythm: still when it rises, moving when it falls. The swordsman of wind and leaves sweeps past you twice and does not see you, because for that moment you are not separate from the wind. When you reach the far side you are trembling, and not from fear.

effects.log: For a breath you were part of the form. You will spend years trying to get back there.
You do not push your luck. Behind you the leaves rise and fall and rise.

events.text: The wind changes just as you move, and suddenly you are standing in the open with the swordsman of wind and leaves before you, its green blade at your throat. It holds there. Then it flicks the tip once against your cheek, a light cut, and blows apart into leaves that sweep you back the way you came.

effects.log: It is very shallow, and perfectly straight. A mark, not a wound. The form remembers you now.
You sit at the edge of the clearing and listen for an hour. It is not random. Next time you will hear it change.

events.text: When the Bamboo Labyrinth closes, the wind stops all at once, and in the silence every stalk begins to bend toward the gate, as if bowing you out. It is very beautiful. It is also somewhat alarming, a whole forest leaning toward you, and you walk out a little faster than you walked in.

effects.log: You turn at the gate and bow to a forest. Nobody else sees. That is all right.
You do not run. Nearly.

events.text: Outside, everyone who came out of the maze is walking strangely: little sways and half-turns, a hand lifting, a foot sliding. The form has got into all of them a little. A gate guard watches the parties stagger past and shakes his head. 'Every twelve years,' he says. 'Takes them a month to walk straight.'

effects.log: You find a quiet corner and walk the sway until it is yours and not the maze's.
He offers you a cup of tea, and the two of you sit and watch the swaying parties go by.

events.text: Your sect's sword masters try for a week to make the bamboo flute do anything at all. It will not cut in their hands. It will not even play. At last they hang it in the sword hall, where the wind from the window sometimes makes it sing, and the juniors stop their practice to listen.

choices.text: Teach the juniors the form you walked

effects.log: You teach them what you can. Some of them start walking strangely, and you count it a success.
You sit under it and listen. It never sings for anyone else quite the same way.

events.text: The ambushers at the maze's gate come out of the bamboo itself, cloaked in green, and when the fight is over they turn out to be no bandits but disciples the barrier threw back. They have waited twelve years to see the form, they say, and took it out on the first person who had.

choices.text: Show them a little of it

effects.log: You show them three steps. They watch with hungry eyes. You have made enemies into something else, perhaps.
They go back into the bamboo. You do not think they will forget your face.

events.text: Somewhere in the maze someone is playing a flute: three notes, a pause, three notes. You follow the sound to a young man sitting cross-legged in a dead end, his eyes clouded white, his head tilted toward the wind. 'Eun Sol,' he says before you speak. 'Outside I am blind. In here the wind in the bamboo tells me every wall.'

effects.log: He tucks the flute in his belt and walks off without hesitating. You follow a blind man through a labyrinth, and do not get lost once.
"They are the maze," he says. "Three notes for each turn. Whoever planted it hummed while he planted. I am only humming it back."
His three notes follow you through the stalks for a long while, and then they are only wind.

events.arc: The Blind Flute of the Labyrinth

events.text: When the wind swordsman has scattered back into leaves, Eun Sol sits down in the clearing and plays a long, slow tune you have never heard. The bamboo leans in to listen. 'That was the form,' he says. 'All of it. I have walked the maze so often I can play it, but I will never hold a sword. Would you like to hear it again?'

effects.log: You close your eyes. With them shut, the tune is a sword moving through leaves: a thrust, a turn, a cut that never quite ends.

choices.text: Ask him to come out with you

effects.log: He is quiet a long time. "Outside, I am blind," he says. "In here, I can see. But I will think about it."

events.arc: The Blind Flute of the Labyrinth

events.text: At the closing gate the wind blows out of the maze, and Eun Sol stands with his face turned into it while the bamboo fades behind him. 'Twelve years in the dark until it opens again,' he says. 'Or I stop coming, and learn to live out there like everyone else. Which would you choose?'

choices.text: Tell him to keep coming back

effects.log: "Then I will see you in twelve years," he says, smiling at a point just past your shoulder. "I will know your step."

choices.text: Offer to be his eyes outside

effects.log: He laughs, startled. "Nobody has offered that before." You walk him to the market road, where he plays the maze's tune for coppers and people stop to listen.

choices.text: Tell him the tune is enough

effects.log: "Yes," he says slowly. "Maybe I can carry the maze with me." He puts the flute to his lips as the gate closes.

events.arc: The Blind Flute of the Labyrinth
